# Aristotelian Motion, Time, and the Temporal Foundations of Rhetorical Being

## 1. Articulate Aristotle's Understanding of Motion and Time

Aristotle's conception of motion (kinesis) and time establishes the foundational framework within which all rhetorical engagement becomes possible, positioning these phenomena not as abstract metaphysical categories but as the very conditions that enable beings to encounter one another meaningfully within shared worlds. When we examine the Aristotelian understanding through contemporary interpretive lenses, particularly those provided by Heidegger's ontological investigations, we discover that motion and time function as the primordial dimensions of what Burke identifies as the dramatistic realm of motivated action (Burke, *A Grammar of Motives*, p. 430-440). The significance of this framework extends beyond theoretical speculation, for it reveals how rhetorical encounters necessarily unfold within temporal horizons that are themselves constituted by the dynamic interplay between potentiality and actuality, between what is and what might become; thus, the rhetorical situation emerges not as a static context but as a fundamentally temporal phenomenon in which speakers and audiences are jointly implicated in processes of becoming that exceed their individual agency while simultaneously depending upon their active participation (Rickert, *Ambient Rhetoric- The Attunements of Rhetorical Being*, pp. 108-109). ## 2. Aristotle on Motion

The Aristotelian conception of motion reveals itself as fundamentally oriented toward the disclosure of being itself, establishing kinesis not merely as change in location but as the primordial way beings comport themselves toward their own possibilities of becoming. Heidegger's  "kinesis is a way of being of beings themselves" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 288), thereby positioning motion as ontologically prior to the traditional subject-object distinctions that have governed subsequent philosophical and rhetorical theory. Within this framework, motion emerges as the dynamic relationality that enables beings to encounter one another within shared temporal horizons; specifically, kinesis manifests as the complex interanimation between what Aristotle identifies as pathesis and poietikos, the capacity to be affected and the capacity to affect, which together constitute what Heidegger recognizes as reaching "into the true center of the Greek view of the world and life" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 26). This understanding transforms our approach to rhetorical analysis, for (White 1985) rhetorical encounters are not transactions between pre-existing subjects but rather emergent events in which speakers and audiences come to be what they are through their mutual involvement in temporal processes of disclosure and concealment (Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, 202b23). ## 3. Aristotle on Time

Aristotelian temporality functions as the enabling condition within which beings can appear to themselves and to one another as determinate entities capable of meaningful interaction, establishing time not as an external container but as the intrinsic dimension of being's self-disclosure. Heidegger's analysis reveals how the Greek understanding of time as connected to being-present (Anwesenheit) provides the foundation for all subsequent determinations of beings in their specific modes of being, including the rhetorical modes through which human beings engage with one another in deliberative, judicial, and epideictic contexts (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 262-263). The temporal structure of being enables what Aristotle recognizes as the discriminating power that must be "one and undivided" in its exercise, suggesting that temporal awareness provides the unified horizon within which all cognitive and perceptual activities become possible (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). Indeed, this temporal foundation becomes particularly significant for understanding how rhetorical discourse can achieve its proper work, for epideictic, deliberative, and judicial genres each presuppose specific temporal orientations that enable speakers to engage audiences in relation to past, present, and future considerations; hence, the effectiveness of rhetorical appeal depends not merely upon logical argumentation or emotional manipulation but upon the temporal attunement that enables speakers and audiences to share a common temporal horizon within which meaningful deliberation becomes possible. ## 4. The Relation Between Motion and Time

The fundamental interrelation between motion and time establishes the ontological ground within which rhetorical activity achieves its proper character as a mode of being-in-the-world that is simultaneously disclosive and constitutive of the situations within which it operates. Burke's analysis of the "temporizing of essence" demonstrates how temporal and logical priority become intertwined in ways that reveal the deeper grammatical incentives underlying rhetorical transformation, particularly in those dramatic forms that seek to disclose the essential nature of human situations through their temporal unfolding (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 27-28). This temporal-kinetic structure enables what Rickert identifies as the ambient dimensions of rhetorical engagement, wherein rhetoric emerges as "an emergent result of many complexly interacting agents dynamically attuned and exposed to one another" within temporal processes that exceed individual conscious control while remaining dependent upon active participation (Rickert, *Ambient Rhetoric- The Attunements of Rhetorical Being*, pp. 53-54). Accordingly, the relation between motion and time provides the foundation for understanding how rhetorical situations achieve their kairotic character, not as opportunities that pre-exist rhetorical engagement but as temporal-kinetic events that emerge through the dynamic interaction between speakers, audiences, and the material circumstances within which their encounters unfold. Subsequently, this understanding transforms our conception of rhetorical agency, revealing it not as the property of individual subjects but as a distributed capacity that emerges through temporal processes of mutual attunement and response. ## 5. Aisthēsis and Temporal Awareness

The Aristotelian understanding of perception (aisthesis) reveals how temporal awareness emerges through the dynamic interaction between sensing beings and their environments, establishing perception not as passive reception but as active temporal engagement that enables beings to orient themselves meaningfully within shared worlds. Heidegger's  the Greek conception of aisthesis provides the foundation for understanding how beings achieve their distinctive capacity for being-in-the-world, a capacity that depends upon temporal awareness as the enabling condition for all subsequent cognitive and practical activities (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). The temporal character of perception becomes particularly significant when we consider how rhetorical engagement presupposes the capacity for what Burke identifies as the "reflexive" function that enables "words about words," the distinctively human capacity for symbolic transformation that emerges through temporal processes of engagement with others (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 302-303). This temporal-perceptual foundation enables speakers and audiences to share common worlds of meaning within which rhetorical appeals can achieve their proper effectiveness; indeed, the success of rhetorical discourse depends upon the establishment of temporal attunement between speakers and audiences, an attunement that enables them to participate jointly in processes of deliberation and judgment that are oriented toward future action while remaining grounded in shared understanding of past and present circumstances. Hence, aisthesis functions not merely as individual sensory capacity but as the intersubjective foundation that enables rhetorical communities to emerge and flourish through temporal processes of mutual recognition and response. ## 6. Phantasia and Temporal Unification

Aristotelian phantasia emerges as the crucial mediating capacity that enables temporal unification within conscious experience, providing the foundation for understanding how rhetorical discourse can achieve its distinctive power to orient human action through the imaginative presentation of possibilities that transcend immediate sensory experience. 115). The temporal character of phantasia becomes particularly evident when we consider how Heidegger interprets the Aristotelian understanding of fear (phobos), which emerges not through direct sensory experience but through imaginative anticipation of future possibilities that achieve their affective power through phantasmatic presentation (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). This imaginative-temporal structure enables what Burke recognizes as the symbolic transformation through which human beings achieve their distinctive capacity for transcending immediate circumstances while remaining oriented toward practical engagement with others in shared temporal contexts (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 27-28). Subsequently, phantasia provides the foundation for understanding how epideictic discourse achieves its proper function of enabling communities to recognize and affirm their shared values through imaginative presentation of exemplary cases that unify past, present, and future within coherent temporal narratives. The unifying power of phantasia thus enables rhetorical discourse to achieve its distinctive capacity for orienting human action through the temporal integration of memory, perception, and anticipation within shared imaginative horizons that exceed individual conscious control while depending upon active communal participation. ## 7. Heidegger's Interpretation of Aristotle

Heidegger's transformative interpretation of Aristotelian philosophy reveals how the traditional metaphysical understanding of motion and time must be reconceived in terms of the more fundamental phenomenon of being-in-the-world, thereby establishing the ontological foundation for understanding rhetoric as a primordial mode of human dwelling rather than merely a technique for persuasive communication. Through his innovative stylistic appropriation of Aristotelian concepts, Heidegger demonstrates how the interanimation of pathesis and poietikos within kinesis discloses the fundamental ambiguity of activity and passivity that characterizes all authentic engagement with beings, an ambiguity that traditional subject-object thinking systematically obscures (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, pp. 26-27). This interpretive approach enables us to recognize how Aristotelian concepts anticipate contemporary insights into the distributed and embedded character of human agency, particularly as these insights emerge through technological developments that challenge traditional boundaries between mind and environment (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 176-177). Heidegger's reading reveals how Aristotle's analysis of the passions (pathe) as Befindlichkeiten or dispositions provides the foundation for understanding rhetorical engagement as fundamentally oriented toward others within shared temporal horizons that enable meaningful deliberation and judgment (Heidegger, *Being and Time*, 1962). Indeed, this interpretation transforms our understanding of what Aristotle means by  human beings are political animals, revealing political existence not as the application of rational capacities to social problems but as the primordial mode of being-with-others that enables the emergence of shared worlds within which rational deliberation becomes possible. Hence, Heidegger's interpretation enables us to recognize how rhetorical theory must move beyond traditional conceptions of persuasion as instrumental manipulation toward a more fundamental understanding of rhetoric as the disclosive activity through which human communities achieve their distinctive capacity for dwelling together within shared temporal horizons that enable both individual flourishing and collective decision-making. ---

## VALIDATION APPENDIX

### Claim Map

*Supporting citations*: Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 27-28; Rickert, *Ambient Rhetoric*, pp. 53-54

**C5**: Aisthesis as temporal engagement enabling being-in-the-world

**C6**: Phantasia as mediating capacity for temporal unification 
*Supporting citations*: O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia*, p. 115; Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115; Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 27-28

**C7**: Heidegger's interpretation reveals rhetoric as primordial dwelling mode
